title: A research pipeline from strategy idea to reproducible backtest in minutes
author: koushik_86
selftext:
This started because I got tired of the same damn loop.

Come up with a strategy hypothesis -> translate it into code -> debug it -> backtest it -> hope it works.

Then realize the hypothesis doesn't even work.

Or worse... somewhere between the research note and the implementation, the idea quietly drifted. A few "small" decisions later, you're no longer testing what you originally had in mind.

That annoyed me enough that I built this.

Describe the strategy in plain english.

The pipeline:

* Translates the idea into a structured strategy specification
* Compiles the spec into deterministic Python
* Runs the backtest
* Performs **walk-forward** validation, **monte carlo** if review passed
* Generates a research report with metrics, trades and equity curve

The design decision I'm happiest with is this:

**The LLM is used ONLY to *translate intent into a validated strategy spec*. Everything after that is deterministic and reproducible**. NO AI-written trading logic. No LLM deciding entries, exits or backtest results. In-built **look-ahead bias prevention**. The backtest and optimization engine is open sourced on github. Tell me if you want link.

In simple words this is **NOT AN AI CODE WRAPPER**, but **THE WHOLE RESEARCH PIPELINE**.

It's still invite-only while preventing high volume of sign-ups and I scale the compute.

https://intellisive.com

No paywall. *I'm literally paying for the compute* because I'd rather get honest feedback from people who actually do systematic research than optimize for signups.

Tear apart the architecture, assumptions, or workflow if you think they're wrong. That's far more useful than "looks cool."

If it sucks, just say it.

comments.author: Ok-Draft2744
comments.body: Interesting concept. Do you use some sort of bulding blocks and ready APIs for indicators? How is the strategy created jf not AI generated code in there? Some sort of configuration is being generated, then translated to strategy which is backtested?

replies.author: koushik_86
replies.body:
Pretty much, yeah.

The language model never generates executable strategy code directly. It produces a validated strategy specification (JSON/schema-based) describing the hypothesis, indicators, entry/exit logic, risk rules, etc.

From there, a deterministic compiler maps those primitives to Python using a library of supported building blocks (indicators, operators, portfolio/risk components, execution assumptions, etc.). The generated code is then backtested and validated.

That separation was intentional. I wanted the language model to translate intent, not invent implementation. It also makes the whole pipeline reproducible.

replies.author: Ok-Draft2744
replies.body: Cool, I hope it takes off!

replies.author: koushik_86
replies.body: Appreciate it! I'd be curious to see where you break it

replies.author: Ok-Draft2744
replies.body:
I've built a simiar system to yours for my own purposes. It uses an llm to translate text to a json configuration and apply all the different technical indicators as fixed functions thta have either been tested previously or are available from a library. I noticed it speeds up my research drastically. 

Where it breaks is when I am exploring a novel idea which has no parallel implementation. This is when I need custom code, which is fine just slower. 

This kind of implementation can get you to the edge/frontier of current strategies pretty quickly with enough experimentation. For example you can use an llm to generate your ideas, and steer them if you know enough about the domain. 

The more advanced version is when you get the llm to generate the ideas, compare the backtest results and then refine automatically. I've had some interesting results there, and smarter models are clearly superior here, think Fable 5.

The most important part for me was making sure the parameters the backtest receives don't give it an option to cheat with forward lookup, e.g. by giving it only the close price. This is more of vanilla backtest problem tho.

replies.body: I started with a CLI too. The pipeline actually began as a CLI because I wanted to keep the workflow scriptable. The difference is that I eventually automated the whole research loop around it instead of treating it as another strategy runner
